title: GeoJSON to CSV Converter: Features to Rows
description: Convert GeoJSON features into a flat CSV table with the GeoJSON to CSV Converter — properties as columns, geometry as coordinate fields. Free, in-browser.
summary_sentence: For example, a FeatureCollection of 1,000 survey points becomes 1,000 spreadsheet rows — one per feature, with the point's longitude and latitude promoted into their own columns.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON to CSV Converter turns a GeoJSON file into a flat table: one row per feature, its properties spread across columns, and its geometry reduced to coordinate fields. Load the file, review the columns, and download a CSV spreadsheets and databases can eat without a GIS in sight.

body.t: The analyst has Excel, not QGIS. Converting the delivery to CSV puts the data in their hands today — the reverse trip is
Point features with flat properties import into any SQL table from CSV. Lines and polygons belong in real geometry columns — see the shape limits in the table on this page.
A CSV opens anywhere, sorts instantly and shows property inconsistencies a map hides — ragged keys, mixed types, missing values.
Once flattened, the file can use this site's CSV instruments — validators, centroid and bounding-box calculators built for tables.

A feature with coordinates [−73.9719, 40.7681] and properties {name: Gate, type: entrance} becomes one row: name=Gate, type=entrance, lon=−73.9719, lat=40.7681. Nothing is invented; the geometry's two numbers take their place as columns.

A LineString of 400 vertices has no single lat/lon. Flattening it means either one row per vertex (a track table) or a text dump of the coordinate list — the converter's handling is stated in its output rather than hidden, and the GPX-style per-vertex table is usually the useful one.

popular_table.note: GeoJSON coordinates are [longitude, latitude] by RFC 7946 — the CSV columns follow that order, and the column names say so, because swapped axes are the conversion's classic injury.

faq: The union of property keys across features, so a key present on only some features still gets its column, with blanks where a feature lacks it. Ragged data survives honestly instead of silently dropping keys.
A feature's id, where present, is carried as a column so rows can be traced back to their source features.
Can rows convert back to GeoJSON?

For point tables, yes — the CSV to GeoJSON Converter reverses the trip. Line and polygon vertex tables need their sequence and ring structure respected, which is why the round trip is guaranteed for points.
Property values keep their JSON types in spirit: numbers write as numbers, strings as text, booleans as true/false. CSV itself is untyped — the receiving program will re-guess, so check imports.
Standard CSV quoting handles them — values containing commas, quotes or newlines are quoted and escaped per RFC 4180 conventions.
The conversion runs in your browser's memory; files in the tens of megabytes usually manage, GIS-scale hundreds of megabytes belong to command-line tools like ogr2ogr.
